citations.claim: Krivitsky, Larman and Flemm's *Org Topologies* primer calls it the Resource topology.
Its purpose is "to ensure that each unit is 100% utilized."
It suits short, specialist engagements.
It isn't built for fast, reliable delivery, and the authors warn that when each part is "optimized in isolation, the performance of the whole system may actually decline."
The Scrum Guide's rule is: "Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making."
The DOE *Human Performance Improvement Handbook* calls human error "the effect or symptom of deeper trouble in the system."
It lists time pressure and distraction among the main conditions that make errors likely, and says: "The organization is perfectly tuned to get the performance it receives from the workforce."
The board that investigated the Columbia shuttle loss found the same pattern at NASA under schedule pressure.
In its words, "The Program was operating too close to too many margins," and such problems "cannot be solved simply by retirements, resignations, or transferring personnel."
The NHS *Just Culture Guide* has a substitution test: would comparable colleagues, under the same conditions, have done the same thing?
In that case "action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate."

The US Forest Service's learning-review guide calls punishing the people involved "the surest way to kill a learning culture," and DOE adds that "A just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting cultu

Jones (*Evidence-based Software Engineering*) cites Goodhart's law: when a measure is used to judge a team, developers get "a motivation to cause the measurements to move in a direction favorable to t
OpenStax's *Principles of Management* adds two cautions.
Goals seen as impossible "lose their motivating effectiveness."
And when people are strongly committed to difficult goals, "good organizational citizenship," such as reviewing a colleague's merge or helping another squad, "is likely to decline."
The *Org Topologies* authors point out that "more output does not mean more outcomes" and that investing to increase output is "suspect."
But Jones also undercuts engineering's claim: people keep using software that has bugs if it gives them enough value.
Systems thinkers describe a pattern called "shifting the burden" (the Brown School systems briefs, after Kim).
A quick fix is "easier and faster than creating an upstream solution," but it can "impede our ability to invest time and energy to the fundamental solution."
Even the most pro-AI source here, the *Org Topologies* primer, says to aim AI at a specific, named bottleneck "over a generic 'adopt AI'."
It also predicts that monitoring AI output "will become an important responsibility for human workers."
Open Kanban's warning: "An exhausted developer, manager or team are the perfect recipe for disaster."
Re-run the portal review so that it asks, in DOE's words, "what could have prevented the event rather than simply concentrating on who caused an event."
The goal-setting research in OpenStax does support hard, specific goals over "do your best."
What applies to us is the same chapter's caveats (impossible goals, goals people haven't accepted, the drop in helping others) plus Goodhart's law.
The just-culture tools (NHS, DOE) keep a route to individual action for reckless or deliberate conduct.
The Forest Service guide builds a firewall: nothing from a learning review feeds discipline.
The Columbia board handled personal accountability in a separate process.
DOE uses root-cause analysis.
The Forest Service guide says "FLAs must avoid causal statements" (an FLA is its facilitated learning analysis, roughly our postmortem).
It also warns that recommendations "add complexity to the workplace, which has the paradoxical effect of increasing risk."
The *Org Topologies* primer argues that expertise is no longer scarce: "Spin up another 10,000 agents."
The systems-thinking and accident-investigation sources treat a technical fix applied to a stressed system as a way to put off the real problem.
Both sides agree on the order, though: fix the org design first, then aim AI.
The same primer says the Resource topology fits some purposes.
The Goodhart line is Jones quoting Goodhart.

ideas.idea: Developers on two or three squads at once pay a switching cost; the fewer things in progress, the faster each finishes
'Nobody idle' optimises utilisation, not flow; pull work from a limited queue instead of pushing to keep people busy
Overflowing sprints: plan to a forecast the team owns, not a target set from above; the Sprint Goal and commitment belong to the Developers
Difficult goals raise effort, but only with commitment and ability; a target with a bonus attached invites gaming the measure
Output isn't outcome: more features shipped doesn't mean the problem customers care about gets solved; feature bloat
A shared Definition of Done is the quality bar; work that doesn't meet it isn't released, which is where the marketing-engineering argument gets settled
Naming and punishing the developer who merged the release: a just-culture test asks whether a peer would have done the same, and treats the system that let it through as the finding
Blame drives reporting underground; the next near-miss won't be surfaced
Buying tools to 'do both' is a fix that fails or shifts the burden: it eases the symptom and leaves the overload in place
The first change is one constraint, not a programme: cut work in progress (or stop the stretch target), then look again
A disagreement among the sources: goal theory says difficult goals improve performance; the flow and respect-for-people sources say overload and unsustainable pace destroy it

note: Most attributions are supported and all qualifying quotations are exact. Partial support: Resource topology delivery claim is broader than the text; agreement on fixing org design before AI overstates the sources; the quoted developer-motivation line is Jones’s explanation of Goodhart, not a quotation of Goodhart. The shared Definition of Done idea is absent; multi-source sentences are scored once, with credited slugs separated by semicolons.
